headline: Wall Street Sees US Hitting $41.1 Trillion Debt Cap in February
author: Alexandra Harris

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Wall Street strategists are bracing for the US Treasury to hit against its borrowing limit as early as February, triggering the need for extraordinary measures before it faces a funding crunch in late 2027.

Strategists at Bank of America Corp., Barclays Plc and Morgan Stanley said that the Treasury's latest financing estimates along with a higher cash balance will pull forward the date it reaches the debt ceiling to mid- to late-February. Bank of America earlier saw the limit would be reached around May.

The US government is less than $800 billion shy of its $41.1 trillion borrowing cap. Treasury's estimates released last week call for roughly $800 billion of net borrowing in the January-to-March period. The department also projected an end-March cash balance of $1 trillion, a record quarter-end target.

The Treasury's increased cash balance likely reflects greater reliance on short-term bills to finance government spending and deficits. Because bill issuance results in larger and more frequent cash outflows during the month, officials generally seek to maintain a larger buffer. That, in turn, uses up the remaining borrowing capacity at a faster rate.

Unless there is an agreement by Congress to raise or suspend the debt limit, the Treasury can avoid breaching it by deploying extraordinary accounting measures that could add an estimated $300 billion to $350 billion before it runs the risk of default.

Strategists, including SMBC Nikko Securities America, expect that the so-called X date — the point at which the Treasury exhausts funds from its cash balance and extraordinary measures and is no longer able to meet all of its obligations — to be sometime between August and November.
The Democratic sweep of Congress raises the prospect of a prolonged confrontation with President Donald Trump over the government's borrowing.

Fitch Ratings warned last month that such an outcome would increase the likelihood of brinkmanship, unless the outgoing Republican-led Congress manages to raise or suspend the debt ceiling before its term expires at year's end.

Debt-limit constraints tend to ripple through funding markets as the Treasury begins drawing down its cash balance and reducing bill issuance. While that temporarily increases reserves in the banking system, putting downward pressure on overnight funding rates, those effects typically reverse once the debt ceiling is resolved. The Treasury will then ramp up bill issuance to replenish its coffers, draining reserves and driving funding costs higher.

An extended standoff next year could disrupt parts of the curve. During past confrontations, investors sold Treasury bills maturing around the date the government was projected to run out of money, while buying securities maturing before or after that date, creating a kink in the curve. Right now, the T-bill curve shows little sign of concern, with the government still months away from hitting the limit.
A delayed resolution could also prolong the Treasury's reliance on short-term borrowing for its overall financing needs and push back efforts to boost issuance of longer maturities later in the year.

"Given how significantly the debt limit could shape money markets next year, over the coming weeks we will be closely watching for progress on the reconciliation process," Barclays strategist Samuel Earl wrote in a note to clients on Friday.
